html:
A huge seated bronze Buddha at the temple of Tōdai-ji in Nara, Japan, dedicated in 752. It is about fifteen metres high and shows Vairocana, the cosmic Buddha.

The emperor Shōmu ordered it in 743, in years of smallpox, famine and revolt. He hoped a Buddha watching over the whole land would protect the state, and he set up official temples in every province, with Tōdai-ji at their head. Casting took years and used much of Japan's copper. At the eye opening ceremony an Indian monk painted in the eyes, before guests from across Asia.

Tōdai-ji was the greatest of Nara's temples and so powerful that the court later moved the capital partly to escape the influence of the Nara monks. The hall was burned in wars in 1180 and 1567. Today's statue is mostly a repair, and the present hall, rebuilt in 1709, is smaller than the first, yet still among the largest wooden buildings in the world.
